lessons.title: 157. Ch 11 · Large numbers and decimals
lessons.subtitle: 만 · 억 · 조 · 삼십오점 일구 · 영점 구 · 사점 공팔

explanations.title: How to read large numbers
explanations.body: In the U.S. we separate every three digits with a comma and name each three-digit group thousand, million, billion, trillion, etc. 304,257,284,567 reads “three hundred four billion, two hundred fifty-seven million, two hundred eighty-four thousand, five hundred sixty-seven.” In Korean we break a number into four-digit groups and name each four-digit group based on 만 (10,000), 억 (100,000,000), 조 (1,000,000,000,000), etc.; however, commas still separate every three digits when a number is in Arabic numerals. The same number is therefore read in four-digit groups: 3,042 억 5,728 만 4,567.

tables.note: Inside a four-digit group the digits are read thousands-hundreds-tens-units; the book writes 3천4십2억 5천7백2십8만 4천5백6십7 (a digit 1 before 천, 백, 십 is not read: 천, 백, 십).

explanations.title: Large numbers from the book and from the chapter
explanations.body: The readings below follow the four-digit rule (the book’s own readings are 백구십이만 육천오백팔 for 1,926,508 and 육만 사백 for 60,400; the others are mine, worked out with the same rule). A 1 before 만 is not read (만), but a 1 before 억 or 조 is (일억, 일조).

explanations.title: How to read decimals
explanations.body: In English, 35.19 is read as “thirty-five point one nine.” Reading decimals in Korean is quite similar. “Point” is read as 점, whose literal meaning is a point or a period. Therefore 35.19 is read as 삼십오점 일구. However, there are some decimal values you should be careful with. For example, .9 and .7 are always rendered as 0.9 or 0.7 in Korean and, therefore, are read as 영점 구 and 영점 칠, respectively. When the number 0 comes after a decimal point, 0 can be read as either 공 or 영; 4.08, for example, is read as 사점 공팔 or 사점 영팔.

explanations.title: Percentages
explanations.body: The book reads percent as 퍼센트 after the number, as in the Activity 3 model: 삼점일 퍼센트 (3.1%) and, in Follow-Up Activity 3 of Topic A, 사십오 퍼센트 (45%).

The headline reads 재미교포 인구 192만명…캘리포니아주에 55만 7천여 명 거주. explanations.title: Part I: checking in at the Olympic Hotel
explanations.body: PV2 Kim is checking in at the front desk of the Olympic Hotel in Koreatown in L.A. The Korean is the book’s, with 120달러, 2개 and 1층 spelled out in Hangul (the English is mine).

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 어서 오세요. 어떻게 도와드릴까요?
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: eoseo oseyo. eotteoke dowadeurilkkayo? — Welcome. How can I help you?

examples.text: 김 이병: 안녕하세요? 빈 방이 있습니까?
examples.translation: gim ibyeong: annyeonghaseyo? bin bangi itseumnikka? — Hello. Do you have a vacant room?

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 네, 있습니다. 언제까지 묵으시겠어요?

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 비 (費)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means expense or fee. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 숙박비, 택시비 and 학비; the answers are below (숙박비 is the lodging fee of the Core Vocabulary; the other two answers are mine).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 실 (室)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a room or chamber, as in 침실 (a bedroom) and 거실 (a living room). The book asks you to guess 세탁실, 화장실 and 교실; the answers are mine.

explanations.title: Role-play plan (Presentation Activity d)
explanations.body: Pair up: one partner plays two customers (PV2 Kim for Part I and PFC Jones for Part II), the other the hotel clerk. As a customer: ask about rooms available for ( ) nights and the room rate; ask about a swimming pool; make a complaint about noise from the next room; make requests for more towels. As a hotel clerk: a hotel room costs ( ) dollars per night; the swimming pool is located next to the emergency exit on the ground floor; accept the customer’s request for a room change. The role-play itself is a partner activity and is not reproduced.

lessons.title: 161. Ch 11 · Grammar A: the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄹ 때 (when)
lessons.subtitle: 숙제할 때 · 날씨가 좋을 때 · 심심할 때 · 점심 때 · 크리스마스 때

explanations.title: -(으)ㄹ 때: “when”
explanations.body: In English, when we use when as a conjunction, as in when he was a boy or when the bell rings, we can translate it as at or during the time that or at the moment that. In Korean we use the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄹ 때 to express when. The same clause is translated differently depending on the main clause: 심심할 때 is “when I am bored”, “when I am bored (in the future)” or “when I was bored”; the tense of the translation is determined by the tense of the main clause, not by 때.

examples.translation: sukjehal ttae tibeuireul an bomnida. — When I do my homework, I don’t watch TV.

explanations.title: How to form -(으)ㄹ 때
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)ㄹ 때. When a verb stem ends in a vowel, add ㄹ 때 (자다 → 잘 때; 심심하다 → 심심할 때). When a verb stem ends in a consonant, add 을 때 (있다 → 있을 때; 먹다 → 먹을 때). The book gives these two cases; the ㄹ-final stems (살다 → 살 때) and the ㅂ irregular stems (춥다 → 추울 때) follow the same pattern as the future attributive form and are mine.

rows: Verb stem ends in a vowel
자다 → 잘 때; 심심하다 → 심심할 때
Verb stem ends in a consonant
있다 → 있을 때; 먹다 → 먹을 때

tables.note: Stems that end in ㄹ keep it (살다 → 살 때), and ㅂ irregular stems change as usual (춥다 → 추울 때); these rows are mine.

explanations.title: 때 is a noun
explanations.body: Although we treat -(으)ㄹ 때 as a conjunctive ending that we often interpret as when, its literal translation is at the time that or at the time of; 때 literally means time, and -ㄹ/을 is an attributive form that modifies the noun 때. Thus, like other nouns, -(으)ㄹ 때 can take a noun marker. Also, the noun 때 is often preceded by a noun that denotes time, like 아침, 점심, 저녁, 크리스마스 and 휴가; in this case 때 can be translated at the time of or during the time of.

lessons.title: 162. Ch 11 · Grammar B: expressing a strong intention with -겠
lessons.subtitle: 저희가 하겠습니다 · 뭘 드시겠습니까? · 비가 오겠습니다 · -겠 vs -(으)ㄹ 거다

explanations.title: -겠: strong possibility and strong intention
explanations.body: In English, the modal verb will, which is used to express an event or a state in the future, implies either the strong possibility of an event/state or the strong intention of the subject: It will rain tonight (strong possibility) versus I will find you! (strong intention). Similarly, the verb suffix 겠 implies the strong possibility of an event/state or the strong intention of the speaker. In an earlier chapter, on weather forecasting, the book briefly discussed that 겠 implies a strong possibility. However, when the subject of a sentence is a person, especially the first or second person, 겠 often conveys the strong intention of the person. The 겠 that conveys the strong intention of the subject is used only with an action verb.

examples.translation: oneul jeonyeogeneun biga ogetseumnida. — It will rain tonight. (strong possibility)
naeireun gureumi kkigetseumnida. — It will be cloudy tomorrow. (strong possibility)
jeohuiga hagetseumnida. — We will do it. (strong intention)
dambaereul kkeunketseumnida. — I will quit smoking. (strong intention)
mwol deusigetseumnikka? — What will you have? (strong intention)
dambaereul kkeunketseumnikka? — Will you quit smoking? (strong intention)

explanations.title: How to form it
explanations.body: Expressing a strong intention: action verb stem + 겠. The book’s example question and answer are below. With the honorific -(으)시- the 시 comes before 겠: 드시겠습니까, 예약하시겠습니까 (my table; 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다).

examples.translation: nuga patireul junbihasigetseumnikka? — Who will prepare for the party?
jega patireul junbihagetseumnida. — I will prepare for the party.

explanations.title: -겠 versus -(으)ㄹ 거다
explanations.body: Recall that -(으)ㄹ 거다, which you learned about in Chapter 9, is also used to express a future event. However, -(으)ㄹ 거다 is usually used to convey a future event that the speaker has prior knowledge of or that has been planned. Thus -(으)ㄹ 거다 is usually translated as “be going to”, while 겠 for intention is “will”.

examples.translation: jeoneun naeil jibe isseul geoyeyo. — I am going to stay home tomorrow.
urineun naenyeone hanguge gal geoyeyo. — We are going to go to Korea next year.

explanations.title: Footnotes: 전에 and 별로
explanations.body: 전에 means previously or before. 별로 means particularly and is always used in a negated sentence, as in 저는 김밥을 별로 안 좋아해요 (I do not particularly like kimbap). The book’s dialog shows both: 전에 써 봤지만 and 별로 싱겁지 않아요.

explanations.title: Types of tastes (맛의 종류)
explanations.body: The book’s table of the five basic tastes. The example sentences are from the Core Vocabulary, except for 맵다, which the book lists in this table but not in its vocabulary list; its example sentence is mine. The last column gives the attributive form used with 맛 (a stative verb’s attributive form ends in (으)ㄴ, as in Chapter 4; the book uses 단 맛, 매운 맛, 짠 맛, 신 맛 and 쓴 맛 in Activity 3).

explanations.title: Cultural notes: table manners and hospitality
explanations.body: A spirit of respect for elders is found throughout Korean culture. People are served in the order of seniority and do not pick up their chopsticks or spoon before elders begin eating. It is also a Korean hospitality custom for hosts to repeatedly urge their guests to eat more. Although the younger generation is slowly moving away from this tradition, many Koreans still practice it. If you wish to stop eating, politely tell your host that you are too full when you are asked to eat more (as PFC Jones does with 배가 불러서 더 못 먹겠어요).

lessons.title: 164. Ch 11 · Grammar C: long-form negation -지 않다 and -지 못하다
lessons.subtitle: 먹지 않아요 · 먹지 못해요 · 춥지 않아요 · 안 vs -지 않다 · 못 vs -지 못하다

explanations.title: Revisiting negation: short and long forms
explanations.body: In Chapter 7 you learned that Koreans negate a verb by placing either 안 or 못 in front of the verb: 아침을 안 먹습니다 (I do not eat breakfast), 아침을 못 먹습니다 (I cannot eat breakfast). 안 and 못 are the short forms of verb negation. In this chapter the book introduces the long forms, -지 않다 and -지 못하다. -지 못하다 is used with an action verb, but is rarely used with a stative verb; it can be used interchangeably with -(으)ㄹ 수 없다.

explanations.title: “Don’t”: verb stem + 지 않다
explanations.body: With verb stems (action verbs and stative verbs), add 지 않다: 일어나다 → 일어나지 않다; 먹다 → 먹지 않다; 춥다 → 춥지 않다.

examples.translation: achime iljjik ireonaji anseumnida. — I don’t get up early in the morning.
jjan eumsigeul meokji anseumnida. — I don’t eat salty foods.
monteureineun chupji anseumnida. — It is not cold in Monterey.

explanations.title: “Can’t”: action verb stem + 지 못하다
explanations.body: With action verb stems only, add 지 못하다: 일어나다 → 일어나지 못하다; 먹다 → 먹지 못하다.

examples.translation: achime iljjik ireonaji motamnida. — I can’t get up early in the morning.
jjan eumsigeul meokji motamnida. — I can’t eat salty foods.
achimeul meogeul su eopseumnida. — I can’t eat breakfast. (= 먹지 못합니다)
jeoneun sureul masiji anayo. — I don’t drink alcohol.
jeoneun sureul masiji motaeyo. — I can’t drink alcohol.
keopineun byeollo masigo sipji anayo. — I don’t particularly want to drink coffee.

explanations.title: Verb tables
explanations.body: The informal polite forms (-지 않아요 and -지 못해요) of action verbs, with the honorific forms, and of stative verbs, which have no -지 못하다 form. The verb tables are mine; the endings are the book’s.

tables.note: Stative verbs are not negated with -지 못하다 (the book: they cannot be negated this way). The ㅂ irregular stems keep ㅂ before 지: 춥지, 맵지.

explanations.title: Follow-Up 1: negate with both forms
explanations.body: The book asks you to negate each verb using both -지 않다 and -지 못하다, remembering that stative verbs cannot be negated with -지 못하다. The book’s models are 회사에 다녀요 → 다니지 않아요, 다니지 못해요 and 돈이 필요합니다 → 필요하지 않아요. The five answers below are mine.

rows: A stative verb: only the -지 않다 form.

explanations.title: Follow-Up 5: rules for a survival game
explanations.body: In the book you are producing the show Survivor and write three things that the staff will not do for the contestants and three things that the contestants cannot do (in the Australian jungle, an island in Indonesia or the Sahara Desert). The book’s models are the first two lines; the other lines are mine.

lessons.title: 165. Ch 11 · Grammar D: the conjunctive ending -지만 (but)
lessons.subtitle: 김치가 맵지만 맛있어요 · 한국말이 어렵지만 재미있어요 · -지만 vs 그렇지만

explanations.title: -지만: contrasting two clauses
explanations.body: In English, when contrasting two clauses we can use conjunctions like but, although and whereas (John works harder, but Jane works smarter). In Korean we contrast two clauses by using the conjunctive ending -지만, which can be interpreted as “but”. It attaches to the verb stem (the past -았/었- comes before it: 추웠지만), and works with both action and stative verbs.

examples.translation: hangugi jakjiman daemaneun deo jagayo. — Korea is small, but Taiwan is smaller.
hangungmari eoryeopjiman jaemiisseoyo. — Korean is difficult, but it is fun.
hangungmari eoryeopjiman jaemiisseoyo. — Although Korean is difficult, it is fun.
gimchiga maepjiman masitseumnida. — Kimchi is spicy, but it is delicious. (the book’s model)

explanations.title: -지만 versus 그렇지만 / 하지만
explanations.body: -지만 may seem identical in meaning to 그렇지만 or 하지만, which you have encountered frequently. The book elaborates on their differences in Chapter 12; for now, know that -지만 is the conjunctive ending and is attached to the verb in the first clause, whereas 그렇지만 or 하지만 are adverbs that come between two independent clauses separated by a period.

examples.translation: hangungmari eoryeowoyo. geureochiman jaemiisseoyo. — Korean is difficult. However, it is fun.

examples.text: 저는 한국 음식을 좋아해요. 그렇지만 제 남편은 일식을 좋아해요.
examples.translation: jeoneun hanguk eumsigeul joahaeyo. geureochiman je nampyeoneun ilsigeul joahaeyo. — I like Korean food. However, my husband likes Japanese food. (the Core Vocabulary’s sentence)

explanations.title: How to form -지만
explanations.body: verb stem + 지만 (the ㅂ irregular stems keep ㅂ here, as before 지: 맵지만, 춥지만). For the past, add 았/었 first: 추웠지만, 비쌌지만. The table is mine.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes pairs together (사업(~하다), ~세(대), 이용(~하다), 체크아웃(~하다), 체크인(~하다), 프런트(데스크), 근무(~하다), 할인(~하다/~받다), 배(가) 부르다); they are split here. The book’s Additional Vocabulary section is a blank list for words you add yourself.

Where a split word has no sentence of its own, it reuses the book’s sentence of the matching word (세대, 할인받다 with a military discount from the hotel review). Digits are respelled in Hangul (3만 → 삼만, 3억 → 삼억, 13억 → 십삼억, 10살 → 열 살, 203호 → 이백삼 호, 3층부터 10층까지 → 삼 층부터 십 층까지, 12층 → 십이 층, 12시 → 열두 시, 120달러 → 백이십 달러); LA is said 엘에이.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify the general profile of the Korean community in the U.S.; use large numbers and decimals in context; make hotel reservations and requests for services; talk about the five basic tastes; identify Korean table etiquette.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -지 않다 (do not); -지 못하다 (cannot); the conjunctive ending -지만 (but); the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄹ 때 (when); -겠 for a strong intention (will); the Sino-Korean syllables 민 (民), 비 (費) and 실 (室).

explanations.title: Notes on the spelling
explanations.body: Koreans write English words in Hangul as they hear them: 재킷 (jacket), 스웨터 (sweater) and 스커트 (skirt) insert the vowel ㅡ between consonant clusters, and 핸드백 is “hand bag”. The book’s Topic B also lists 치마, a native Korean word for a skirt, next to the loan word 스커트.

explanations.title: Journal: a gift shop and a post office in L.A.
explanations.body: The following text is SPC Jones’ journal entry about her shopping at a gift shop and sending parcels at a post office in L.A. The Korean is the book’s, with the prices and counted numbers spelled out in Hangul (120불 → 백이십 불, 60불, 20불, 10장 → 열 장, 2장 → 두 장, 19불 → 십구 불; the English is mine).

examples.text: 어제 부모님 선물을 사러 선물 가게에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: eoje bumonim seonmureul sareo seonmul gagee gatseumnida. — Yesterday I went to a gift shop to buy presents for my parents.

examples.text: 아버지 선물로 지갑을 샀고 어머니 선물로 귀걸이를 샀습니다.

explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary). The book lists -게 (the adverb maker, explained in its own lesson), ~불 and ~장 (counters), and 포장(하다) as a group; 벨트 and 핸드백 are loan words. 친절하다 is the verb of 친절 “kindness”.

explanations.title: Counters: 불 and 장
explanations.body: 불 counts dollars (the book also writes ~달러; in speech both are used) and 장 counts sheets of paper, cloth, postcards, stamps, etc. Both come after a number: Sino-Korean numbers with 불 (십구 불) and native numbers with 장 (열 장, 두 장). In the journal: 우표 열 장과 엽서 두 장 (ten stamps and two postcards).

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: 원래 /월래/
explanations.body: Have you noticed that 원 in 원래 sounds like 월? This is due to the influence of the consonant ㄹ in the syllable that follows. When ㄴ is followed by ㄹ, oftentimes ㄴ changes into ㄹ. This is an example of anticipatory assimilation, in which a sound becomes more like a following sound. The book’s practice words are in the table.

explanations.title: Cultural note: the Korean postal system
explanations.body: The Korean postal system is different from that in the U.S. with regard to outgoing mail. The U.S. postal system usually picks up outgoing mail from home addresses, but the postal system in Korea does not. Therefore, when Koreans have outgoing mail they go to the post office or post their letters in a red mailbox on the street, which is called 우체통.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 우 (郵)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable 우 means post or mail, as in 우체국 (a post office), 우표 (post stamp; “post ticket”), 우편물 (mail; postal matter) and 우편번호 (the postal code; zip code; “postal number”).

explanations.title: Korean verbs that express “to wear” or “to put on”
explanations.body: Korean uses a different verb depending on the kind of item. 입다 is for basic clothing items; 신다 for footwear; 쓰다 for items worn to cover the head or face; 매다 (“to tie”) for items worn by tying; 끼다 (“to insert”) for items that are snug-fitting; and 차다 (“to fasten”) for items worn by fastening them on. Some items take more than one verb (안경 can take 쓰다 or 끼다). In the book’s table 마스크 means “a mask”, 총 “a gun” and 수통 “a canteen”; the others are in the list above or in the Core Vocabulary.

lessons.title: 173. Ch 12 · Grammar A: asking for and giving permission with -아/어도 되다
lessons.subtitle: 입어 봐도 돼요? · 먹어도 돼요? · 앉아도 되다 · 봐도 되다 · 해도 괜찮아요

explanations.title: -아/어도 되다: “may I …?”
explanations.body: In English, we use phrases such as “May I …?”, “Is it all right if …?” or “Do you mind if …?” when asking for permission; the same phrases are used when permission is granted (“You may …” or “It’s all right if …”). In Korean, we use -아/어도 되다 when asking for or giving permission to do something. 되다 literally means “to become”; it can also mean to be O.K., to be fine, to be all right or to be possible. Therefore -아/어도 좋다 and -아/어도 괜찮다 can be substituted for -아/어도 되다.

examples.translation: gyosireseo yeongeoreul haedo dwaeyo? — Is it all right if I speak English in the classroom?

explanations.title: How to form it
explanations.body: verb stem + 아/어도 되다 (괜찮다/좋다). If the last syllable of the verb stem contains the vowels ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아도 되다; if it contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ, add 어도 되다. The usual contractions of the -아/어 form apply (보다 → 봐도, 마시다 → 마셔도, 하다 → 해도, 쓰다 → 써도).

rows: The last syllable of a verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
의자에 앉다 → 의자에 앉아도 되다; 영화를 보다 → 영화를 봐도 되다
The last syllable of a verb stem contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
코트를 입다 → 코트를 입어도 되다; 책을 읽다 → 책을 읽어도 되다

lessons.title: 174. Ch 12 · Grammar B: denying permission with -(으)면 안 되다
lessons.subtitle: 영어를 하면 안 됩니다 · 주차하면 안 돼요 · 앉으면 안 되다 · 놀면 안 돼

explanations.title: -(으)면 안 되다: “you may not …”
explanations.body: To express a refusal of permission or the prohibition of an action, Koreans use -(으)면 안 되다. The literal meaning of -(으)면 안 되다 is “(it) is not all right if …” or “(it) is not fine if …”. Thus, depending on the context, it can be translated as you may not, you should not, you must not or you are not allowed to.

examples.translation: gyosireseo yeongeoreul hamyeon an doemnida. — You should not speak English in the classroom.
igose juchahamyeon an dwaeyo. — You may not park your car here.
doseogwaneseo eumsigeul meogeumyeon an doemnida. — You must not eat in the library. (the Core Vocabulary’s sentence)

explanations.title: How to form it
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)면 안 되다. When the verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ, add 면 안 되다 (기숙사에 살다 → 기숙사에 살면 안 되다; 친구를 만나다 → 친구를 만나면 안 되다). When the verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ, add 으면 안 되다 (여기에 앉다 → 여기에 앉으면 안 되다; 창문을 닫다 → 창문을 닫으면 안 되다). The ㄷ irregular verb 듣다 changes to 들으면 (음악을 들으면 안 되다); this is mine.

rows: The verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ
기숙사에 살다 → 기숙사에 살면 안 되다; 친구를 만나다 → 친구를 만나면 안 되다
The verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ
여기에 앉다 → 여기에 앉으면 안 되다; 창문을 닫다 → 창문을 닫으면 안 되다

explanations.title: Dependent nouns: 데 (a place) and 것 (a thing)
explanations.body: The two nouns -데 (a place) and -것 (a thing) are called dependent nouns because they cannot stand on their own and must be accompanied by a modifier immediately preceding them. While both nouns can be modified by the attributive forms of verbs, as in 먹을 데 (a place to eat) and 먹을 것 (a thing to eat), -것 can also be modified by a demonstrative, as in 이것 (this thing) and 저것 (that thing). However, -데 cannot be modified by a demonstrative. The dialog uses both: 고기 파는 데 and 더 필요한 것.

lessons.title: 176. Ch 12 · Grammar C: the “adverb maker” -게
lessons.subtitle: 싸게 · 바쁘게 · 예쁘게 · 맛있게 · 예쁘게 포장해 주세요

explanations.title: -게: making an adverb
explanations.body: Adverbs are words that modify (describe) verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, as in work hard, truly happy or extremely slowly. Like truly and extremely, many English adverbs end in -ly; we know that these adverbs are derived from adjectives (true and extreme), and we make them adverbs by adding -ly, so -ly is an adverb “maker”. Korean has an adverb maker as well: 게. Simply by adding 게 to the stem of a stative verb, we make it an adverb: 싸게 (cheaply), 바쁘게 (busily).

lessons.title: 177. Ch 12 · Grammar D: connectors for sentences, verbs and nouns
lessons.subtitle: 그리고 · 그렇지만 · 하지만 · 그러나 · 그런데 · 그래서 · -고 · -지만 · -(으)면 · ~와/과 · ~(이)나

explanations.title: Three types of connectors
explanations.body: You have learned quite a few connectors so far. They are categorized into three types: sentence connectors, verb connectors (or conjunctive endings) and noun connectors.

explanations.title: 1. Sentence connectors
explanations.body: Sentence connectors connect two independent clauses: 저는 초콜렛을 좋아합니다. 그리고 제 친구도 초콜렛을 좋아합니다. / 저는 초콜렛을 좋아합니다. 하지만 제 친구는 안 좋아합니다. (I like chocolate. And my friend likes chocolate too. / I like chocolate. But my friend doesn’t.) The book’s list is below; the English meanings are the book’s.

rows: 어제 영화를 봤어요. 그리고 쇼핑도 했어요.
이 옷은 너무 비싸요. 그렇지만 마음에 들어요.
이 옷은 너무 비싸요. 하지만 마음에 들어요.
오늘은 학교에 가는 날입니다. 그러나 집에서 쉬겠습니다.
내일 산호세 가서 쇼핑하자. 그런데, 한국식품점은 몇 시에 열어?
어제 늦게까지 공부했어. 그래서 좀 피곤해.

explanations.title: 2. Verb connectors (conjunctive endings)
explanations.body: Verb connectors connect two clauses or verbs: 먹습니다 + -고 + 마십니다 → 먹고 마십니다; 저는 공부합니다 + -(으)ㄹ 때 + 음악을 듣습니다 → 저는 공부할 때 음악을 듣습니다. The book’s list is below.

rows: 이 옷은 너무 비싸지만 마음에 들어요.
저녁에 한국 식당 가서 밥 먹자. 이번 주말은 바빠서 등산 못 가요.
다음주에 시험이 있기 때문에 이번 주말에 공부를 해야 합니다.
피곤하면 오늘은 운동하지 마세요. 큰 하얀 건물이 나오면 우회전 하세요.
저는 영화 볼 때 늘 팝콘을 먹어요.

explanations.title: 3. Noun connectors
explanations.body: Noun connectors connect nouns. In English, when we enumerate two or more nouns, we tend to use and/or before the last noun. However, Koreans tend to repeat the noun connector after every noun, as in 포도하고 딸기하고 사과, which translates as “grapes and strawberries and apples”.

rows: 마켓에서 고기와 양념과 과일을 좀 샀습니다. 백화점에서 청바지하고 티셔츠를 세일해요. 생선이랑 소고기랑 닭고기가 모두 얼마에요?
한국 음식이나 멕시코 음식을 먹고 싶어요.

explanations.title: -지만 versus 그렇지만 (from Chapter 11)
explanations.body: As the book said in Chapter 11, -지만 is a conjunctive ending attached to the verb in the first clause, whereas 그렇지만 and 하지만 are adverbs that come between two independent clauses separated by a period. The same holds for the other pairs: -고 / 그리고, -기 때문에 / 그래서.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes some words as groups (포장(~하다), 계산(~하다), 식품(점), 친절(~하다), 그럼(요)); they are split here, and a word without a sentence of its own reuses the book’s. The book’s Additional Vocabulary section is a blank list for words you add yourself.

Digits are respelled in Hangul (5분 → 오 분, 70세 → 칠십 세, 10장 → 열 장, 2파운드 → 두 파운드, 1달러는 100센트 → 일 달러는 백 센트, 50센트 → 오십 센트, 70달러 → 칠십 달러, 50불 → 오십 불, 100달러 → 백 달러, 95불 → 구십오 불); the possessive 의 after a thing is said 에 (후추의 → 후추에). 총 and 수통 are not in the Core Vocabulary; they appear in the table of the “wear” verbs.

explanations.title: What Chapter 13 teaches (한국에 오신 것을 환영합니다)
explanations.body:
Chapter 13, “Welcome to Korea”, opens Unit 4 of the Semester 1 Student’s Edition (A Visit to Korea, 한국 방문). It has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about flight information including date, time, and flight number; comprehend and respond to flight announcements; understand the boarding procedures at an international airport; answer questions at the customs and immigration office; request in-flight services; request information about airport facilities and services; and describe the size, color, and shape of objects.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the noun connector ~(이)나 (or); expressing total negation with 아무 ~도; the conjunctive ending -(으)려고 (in order to; so as to); the conjunctive ending -(으)려면 (if one intends to, if one plans to); and the Sino-Korean syllables 권 (券), 승 (乘), 착 (着), and 면 (免).

explanations.title: Topic A: At the International Terminal
explanations.body: The text is SPC Anderson’s journal entry about his first international flight experience at San Francisco International Airport. (The English is mine. The book writes the flight number as KE024편; Latin letters and digits are respelled in Hangul here, 케이이공이사편.)

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 승 (乘)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means riding or getting on (a flight, ship, bus, rollercoaster, horse, etc.), as in 탑승 (boarding; embarkation), 승객 (a passenger; “riding guest”), 승용차 (a car; “vehicle for riding use”), and 승무원 (a crew member; a flight attendant; “riding and working member”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 승차, 승마 and 승선; my answers are in the last card.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): before boarding
explanations.body: The book shows check-in and boarding instructions written on the back of a boarding pass and asks you to put the steps in order. explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic B
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter). The book writes 기내(식), 신고(하다), 연착(하다/되다), 입국(하다), 착륙(하다), 출국(하다), 통과(하다) and 물어보다 / 묻다 with the optional parts in parentheses; the optional parts are kept in the meanings here.

rows: (申告) report; declaration (~하다: to report; to declare)
(延着) late arrival; delay in arrival (~하다/되다: to be delayed; to be late)
(入國) entry into a country (~하다: to enter a country)
(着陸) landing; “on the land” (~하다: to land)
(出國) departure from the country (~하다: to depart from the country)
(出入國) the leaving and entering of a country
(通過) passing through (~하다: to pass through)

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 착 (着)
explanations.body: The underlying meaning of this Sino-Korean syllable is physical contact or touch (with a larger object). Depending on the context it can translate to touch, stick to, put on (clothes, hat, shoes, etc.), or arrive, as in 착륙 (landing; “come into contact with land”), 착용 (putting on a safety belt; “putting on and using”), 도착 (arrival), 연착 (delayed arrival), etc.

rows: putting on a safety belt; “putting on and using”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 면 (免)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means escape, avoid, or exempt, as in 면세 (tax exemption), 면역 (immunity; “exemption from diseases”), and 면허 (a license; a permit; “exempt from permission”). Note that 면허, which literally means “exempt from permission”, refers to a license or permit, as in 운전면허 (driver’s license) and 사업면허 (business license). How can this be? When you get 면허, you are exempt from further permission from authorities and you have your own license to enjoy!

rows: a license; a permit; “exempt from permission”

lessons.subtitle: 한식이나 일식 · 지갑이나 벨트 · 사과나 배 · 샌프란시스코나 산호세

explanations.title: The noun connector ~(이)나 (or)
explanations.body: As the name suggests, the noun connector ~(이)나 is used to connect nouns and is translated as “or” or “either … or”: 샌프란시스코나 산호세 ((either) San Francisco or San Jose), 한국말이나 일본말 ((either) Korean or Japanese). When a noun ends in a consonant add 이나 (한식이나 일식, 지갑이나 벨트, 사과나 배); when a noun ends in a vowel add 나 (샌프란시스코나 산호세).

lessons.title: 184. Ch 13 · Grammar B: total negation with 아무 ~도
lessons.subtitle: 아무도 · 아무것도 · 아무 데도 · 아무 책도 · 하나도 · 한 명도

explanations.title: Partial and total negation
explanations.body:
Compare the two English sentences “We do not need all the apples for the pie” and “We do not need any apples for the pie”. The first indicates that some but not all apples are needed, which is a partial negation; the second indicates that no apples are needed, which is a total negation.

In Korean we can express a total negation as: 아무도 / 아무 noun도 … negative verb. Since 아무 means “anyone” or “any” and the marker 도 means “even” or “also”, the translations are “… not meet … even one person”, “… not read … even one book”, “… not go … even one place” and “… not do … even one thing”.

examples.translation: jinan jumare amudo an mannasseoyo. — Last weekend, I didn’t meet anyone.

explanations.title: Adding another marker
explanations.body: If we have to add an additional marker, such as 에서, 에, 한테, or (으)로, to 아무 (noun)도, the marker comes right before 도: 아무한테도 ((not) … to any one), 아무 곳에서도 ((not) … at any place), 아무 펜으로도 ((not) … with any pen).

explanations.title: 하나도 and 한 명도
explanations.body: We can also express a total negation by using 하나도 (even one), 한 명도 (even one person), etc.: 저는 취미가 하나도 없어요 (I don’t have even one hobby); 교실에 학생이 한 명도 없어요 (There isn’t even one student in the classroom).

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a traveler’s guide on in-flight duty-free items
explanations.body: The excerpt is from a traveler’s guide. The book asks you to answer four questions in English: list at least four items sold in-flight; where you can find a catalog of duty-free items; when you can start buying; and to translate the underlined sentence (which one is underlined cannot be seen in the text, so all four sentences are translated below). The text is the book’s; the English is mine.

examples.text: 국제선 비행기를 타면 기내 면세점 서비스를 이용할 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: gukjeseon bihaenggireul tamyeon ginae myeonsejeom seobiseureul iyonghal su itseumnida. — If you take an international flight, you can use the in-flight duty-free shop service.

examples.text: 기내 면세품으로는 화장품이 가장 많고 액세서리(시계, 목걸이), 담배, 초콜릿, 볼펜 등도 있습니다.
examples.translation: ginae myeonsepumeuroneun hwajangpumi gajang manko aekseseori(sigye, mokgeori), dambae, chokollit, bolpen deungdo itseumnida. — Among in-flight duty-free items, cosmetics are the most, and there are also accessories (watches, necklaces), cigarettes, chocolate, ballpoint pens and so on.

examples.text: 기내 면세품 카탈로그는 좌석 앞쪽 포켓에 있습니다.
examples.translation: ginae myeonsepum katallogeuneun jwaseok apjjok pokese itseumnida. — The catalog of in-flight duty-free items is in the pocket in front of your seat.

examples.text: 면세품은 보통 첫 번째 기내식 후에 살 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: myeonsepumeun botong cheot beonjjae ginaesik hue sal su itseumnida. — You can usually buy duty-free items after the first in-flight meal.

explanations.title: The answers (mine)
explanations.body:
1. Items sold in-flight: cosmetics (the most), accessories (watches, necklaces), cigarettes, chocolate and ballpoint pens. 2. The catalog is in the pocket in front of the seat. 3. You can usually start buying after the first in-flight meal.

The book does not translate the words of the excerpt; the meanings below are mine.

explanations.title: North Korea report
explanations.body: A cellular phone is called 손전화 (“hand phone”) in North Korea, where the use of such phones has been restricted for residents. Foreign tourists who travel there are required to surrender their mobile phones upon arrival. These phones are then sealed and returned only when departing the country. In early 2009, North Korea launched a new cellular phone service that restricts communication to within North Korea only. Subscribers are not able to call or accept calls from outside the country.

lessons.title: 187. Ch 13 · Grammar C: -(으)려고 (in order to)
lessons.subtitle: 타려고 · 살려고 · 찾으려고 · 먹으려고 · 사려고 · 예약하려고

explanations.title: Conjunctive endings that express a purpose or intention: -(으)려고
explanations.body:
In Chapter 6 you learned that the conjunctive ending -(으)러 is used to express a purpose or intention, as in 식당에 식사하러 오다 (come to the restaurant to eat) and 숙제하러 도서관에 가다 (go to the library to do homework). However, -(으)러 works only with verbs like 가다, 오다 or 다니다. To express a purpose or intention that can work with any action verb (containing 가다, 오다 and 다니다 in the main clause), we can use the conjunctive ending -(으)려고, translated as “(in order) to; so as to”.

When a verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ add 려고 (타다 → 타려고; 살다 → 살려고); when it ends in a consonant other than ㄹ add 으려고 (찾다 → 찾으려고; 먹다 → 먹으려고).

rows: A verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ
A verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ

lessons.title: 188. Ch 13 · Grammar D: -(으)려면 (if one intends to)
lessons.subtitle: 타려면 · 살려면 · 찾으려면 · 먹으려면 · 환전하려면 어떻게 해야 해요?

explanations.title: Conditional with intention or wish: -(으)려면
explanations.body:
In Chapter 9 you learned that the conjunctive ending -(으)면 expresses a conditional (“if” or “when”), as in 약을 먹으면 (if I take medicine). -(으)려면 is another conjunctive ending that expresses a conditional, but one with intention or wish; it can be translated as “if [the subject] plans to / intends to / would like to / wishes to”. It is a contraction of -(으)려고 하면.

When a verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ add 려면 (타다 → 타려고 하면 → 타려면; 살다 → 살려고 하면 → 살려면); when it ends in a consonant other than ㄹ add 으려면 (찾다 → 찾으려고 하면 → 찾으려면; 먹다 → 먹으려고 하면 → 먹으려면).

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): the Airport Service Center Q&A
explanations.body: The text is from the Q&A section of the Lost & Found department of the Airport Service Center website. The book asks you to fill in a table in English (the writer’s concern, the actions requested, the items mentioned by the center, the location and the number of the center). explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. In the book the optional parts, such as (~하다/되다) or (선), are written in parentheses; they are kept in the meaning cells here.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (OZ045편 → 오지공사오편, KE024편 → 케이이공이사편, 8번 → 팔 번, 1층 → 일 층); the book’s English glosses inside a few examples, such as 외국(foreign country), are left out. The book spells “iPad” 아이파드; that spelling is kept. The book’s Additional Vocabulary table is empty: it is for your own words.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: talk about flight information including date, time, and flight number; comprehend and respond to flight announcements; understand the boarding procedures at an international airport; answer questions at the customs and immigration office; request in-flight services; request information about airport facilities and services; describe the size, color, and shape of objects.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the noun connector ~(이)나 (or); expressing total negation with 아무 ~도; the conjunctive ending -(으)려고 (in order to; so as to); the conjunctive ending -(으)려면 (if one intends to, if one plans to); the Sino-Korean syllables 권 (券), 승 (乘), 착 (着), and 면 (免).

explanations.title: What Chapter 14 teaches (한국의 대중 교통)
explanations.body:
Chapter 14, “Public Transportation in Korea”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: ask for information about public transportation in Korea; read subway line maps and signs to get around using the subway system; comprehend and respond to public announcements in the subway; read traffic signs; ask for and give directions; and talk about public transportation in Korea.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -고 있다, which is used to express an action in progress; -기 바라다, which is used to give public instruction (please …); the conjunctive ending -(으)니까 (because); ㄷ irregular verbs; and the Sino-Korean syllables 차 (車), 금 (禁), and 도 (道).

explanations.title: Strategy: study the origins of words (etymology)
explanations.body: Sino-Korean words make up about 60% of the Korean vocabulary (H. Sohn, The Korean Language, Cambridge University Press 2001). Therefore, knowledge of Sino-Korean roots is a must for systematically expanding and retaining Korean words. Recall the Sino-Korean word 승무원 (乘務員), meaning a crew member or flight/train/bus/ship attendant, which we learned in Chapter 13. Each individual syllable of the word has a meaning: 승 (乘) means to ride, 무 (務) work, and 원 (員) a member. Once we get to know the meanings of these individual syllables, it is not difficult to figure out the meanings of newly encountered words that contain one of the syllables. For example, when we encounter the words 승차, 사무실 and 공무원, we can figure out their meanings relatively easily.

explanations.title: The same sound, different Chinese characters
explanations.body: Depending on what Chinese character the syllable comes from, however, the syllable can be interpreted differently. For example, 원 in 공무원 (a public servant) or 승무원 (a crew member) is interpreted as a member because it comes from the Chinese character 員 (원), whereas 원 in 병원 (a hospital) is interpreted as a house because it comes from the Chinese character 院 (원). Notice that both are spelled the same in Korean, although their Chinese characters are different and thus their meanings are different. This is why the book provides Hanja (Chinese characters) next to every Sino-Korean core vocabulary item in the Core Vocabulary sections from Unit 4 on. (The 病 in 병원 and the 室 in 사무실 are mine; the book gives the Hanja only for 員 and 院.)

explanations.title: Topic B, part I: at the ticket booth
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is talking to a subway employee at a ticket booth in the Incheon International Airport Railroad station. (The English is mine; the book writes 5호선 and 2호선, spelled out as 오 호선 and 이 호선.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 저, 실례합니다. 서울대학교 입구까지 어떻게 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: jeo, sillyehamnida. seouldaehakgyo ipgukkaji eotteoke gayo? — Excuse me. How do I get to the entrance of Seoul National University?

examples.text: 지하철 직원: 먼저 공항철도를 타고 김포공항역에서 내리세요. 거기서 광화문 방면으로 가는 지하철 오 호선으로 갈아타세요.
examples.translation: jihacheol jigwon: meonjeo gonghangcheoldoreul tago gimpogonghangyeogeseo naeriseyo. geogiseo gwanghwamun bangmyeoneuro ganeun jihacheol o hoseoneuro garataseyo. — First take the airport railroad and get off at Gimpo Airport Station. From there, transfer to the Line 5 subway that goes in the direction of Gwanghwamun.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 오 호선을 탄 후에는 어디서 내려요?

examples.text: 지하철 직원: 영등포구청역에서 내려서 이 호선으로 갈아타세요.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 차 (車)
explanations.body: The Chinese character 車 of the syllable depicts the shape of a cart seen from above: the two parallel horizontal lines are wheels and the vertical line is the axle, which carries the body (box) of the cart. Thus the meaning of this syllable is a cart, car, or vehicle on wheel(s), as in 자동차 (an automobile; “self-moving car”), 전동차 (a subway; an electric car; “electricity moving car”), 기차 (a train; “steam car”), 무개차 (a convertible; “no cover car”), etc. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 차도, 차창, 차선, 소형차 and 차비; my answers are in the second table.

explanations.title: North Korea report
explanations.body: The subway is called 지하철도 (underground railroad) in North Korea. Pyongyang Metro is an important part of the transportation infrastructure in the capital of North Korea. It was constructed with close attention to security and was first opened in September 1973. It is connected to secret underground military facilities; as a result, the system can serve as a bunker. However, relatively little is known about the Metro outside the country, as few visitors are able to investigate the system.

lessons.title: 195. Ch 14 · Grammar A: an action in progress with -고 있다
lessons.subtitle: 보고 있어요 · 먹고 있어요 · 공부하고 있었어요 · 운동하고 있을 거예요 · 보고 계세요

explanations.title: Expressing an action in progress
explanations.body:
In English we commonly use “to be -ing” to express an action in progress, as in “I am working” or “Thomas is driving”. In Korean we use -고 있다 (added to the stem of an action verb): 지금 신문을 보고 있어요 (I am reading the newspaper now); 지금 점심식사를 하고 있어요 (I am having lunch now).

계시다 is the honorific form of 있다. Thus we can use -고 계시다 to describe an action being done by a person we have to show respect to: 아버님이 신문을 보고 계십니다 (Father is reading the newspaper); 선생님이 점심식사를 하고 계십니다 (The teacher is having lunch). -고 있었다 is used for a past progressive action and -고 있을 것이다 for a future progressive action.

rows: After the stem of an action verb
먹다 → 먹고 있다; 자다 → 자고 있다
tables.title: action verb stem + 고 있다

lessons.title: 196. Ch 14 · Grammar B: public instructions with -기(를) 바라다
lessons.subtitle: 이용하시기 바랍니다 · 기다리시기를 바랍니다 · 갈아타시기 바랍니다 · 건강하시기를 바랍니다

explanations.title: Giving instructions using -기(를) 바라다
explanations.body:
-기(를) 바라다 literally means “(I) hope (you) to …” and we can say it to an individual to mean “I wish you to …” or “I hope that you …”, as in 건강하시기(를) 바랍니다 (“I wish you to be healthy” or “I hope you are healthy”). However, we often hear -기(를) 바라다 in announcements made at public places like an airport, subway station, or department store. In this case, we can interpret it as an instruction that can be translated as “it is desirable that”, “we advise you that”, or “please”; for example, 에스컬레이터를 이용하시기(를) 바랍니다 (Please use the escalator) and 자동판매기를 사용하시기 바랍니다 (Please use the vending machines).

Note that the honorific form -(으)시기 바라다 is normally used for a public announcement. Note also that the object marker can be deleted (as in -기 바라다). In addition, -기를 is often contracted to -길 in speaking.

rows: 이용하다 → 이용하기(를) 바라다; 기다리다 → 기다리기(를) 바라다

lessons.title: 197. Ch 14 · Activities B: a subway trip and how to get to a restaurant
lessons.subtitle: 오산에서 이대까지 · 갈아타는 곳 표지판을 따라 · 명화당 찾아 오시는 길 · 논현역에서 칠 호선

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading and writing): photos of the Seoul subway
explanations.body: The book shows eight photos from the Seoul Metropolitan Subway stations and asks you to write, in Korean and English, what each photo shows. The photos are pictures; the words that go with such signs are in the Core Vocabulary lessons of this chapter (금연, 출입금지, 승강장, 매표소, 자동판매기, 계단, 줄, 정거장).

explanations.title: Activity 1b (Reading): a student’s subway trip from Osan to Ewha
explanations.body: The passage is about a student’s experience using the Seoul Metro Subway from Osan to E-Dae (Ewha Women’s University) station. The book gives the eight sentences in scrambled order and asks you to arrange them in the order in which they occurred; three are done for you (the first, 5, and the last, 8). The sentences are the book’s (the numbers 1, 2 are spelled out); the English is mine, and the order is shown here in the right sequence.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 지하철을 타고 이대 앞에 사는 친구 집에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: jinan jumare jihacheoreul tago idae ape saneun chingu jibe gatseumnida. — Last weekend I went by subway to the home of a friend who lives in front of Ewha Women’s University. (sentence 1)

examples.text: 먼저 오산 지하철역에 도착해서 자동판매기에서 승차권을 샀습니다.
examples.translation: meonjeo osan jihacheoryeoge dochakaeseo jadongpanmaegieseo seungchagwoneul satseumnida. — First I arrived at Osan subway station and bought a ticket at the vending machine. (sentence 2)

examples.text: 승차권을 산 후에 에스컬레이터를 타고 승강장으로 내려갔습니다.
examples.translation: seungchagwoneul san hue eseukeolleiteoreul tago seunggangjangeuro naeryeogatseumnida. — After buying the ticket, I went down to the platform by escalator. (sentence 3)

examples.text: 승강장에서 줄을 서서 기다린 후에 서울역 방면 일 호선 전동차를 탔습니다.
examples.translation: seunggangjangeseo jureul seoseo gidarin hue seoullyeok bangmyeon il hoseon jeondongchareul tatseumnida. — After standing in line and waiting on the platform, I took the Line 1 train toward Seoul Station. (sentence 4)

examples.text: 일 호선을 타고 한 시간쯤 후에 신도림역에서 내렸습니다.
examples.translation: il hoseoneul tago han siganjjeum hue sindorimyeogeseo naeryeotseumnida. — After about an hour on Line 1, I got off at Sindorim Station. (sentence 5)

examples.text: 신도림역에서 내린 후에 갈아타는 곳 표지판을 따라 시청방면 이 호선으로 갈아탔습니다.
examples.translation: sindorimyeogeseo naerin hue garataneun got pyojipaneul ttara sicheongbangmyeon i hoseoneuro garatatseumnida. — After getting off at Sindorim Station, I followed the transfer sign and transferred to Line 2 toward City Hall. (sentence 6)

examples.text: 이 호선을 타고 몇 정거장을 더 간 후에 이대역에서 내렸습니다.
examples.translation: i hoseoneul tago myeot jeonggeojangeul deo gan hue idaeyeogeseo naeryeotseumnida. — After riding Line 2 for a few more stations, I got off at Ewha Women’s University Station. (sentence 7)

examples.text: 이대역에서 내린 후 일 번 출구로 나갔습니다.
examples.translation: idaeyeogeseo naerin hu il beon chulguro nagatseumnida. — After getting off at Ewha Station, I went out through exit number 1. (sentence 8)

explanations.title: The order (mine)
explanations.body: The numbers below are the right order of the actions.

rows: 지난 주말에 지하철을 타고 이대 앞에 사는 친구 집에 갔습니다.
먼저 오산 지하철역에 도착해서 자동판매기에서 승차권을 샀습니다.
승차권을 산 후에 에스컬레이터를 타고 승강장으로 내려갔습니다.
승강장에서 줄을 서서 기다린 후에 서울역 방면 일 호선 전동차를 탔습니다.
일 호선을 타고 한 시간쯤 후에 신도림역에서 내렸습니다.
신도림역에서 내린 후에 갈아타는 곳 표지판을 따라 시청방면 이 호선으로 갈아탔습니다.
이 호선을 타고 몇 정거장을 더 간 후에 이대역에서 내렸습니다.
이대역에서 내린 후 일 번 출구로 나갔습니다.

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading and writing): how to get to a famous restaurant
explanations.body: The book shows an advertisement for a famous restaurant and asks you to circle the stations at which you should get off to get to it. The text is the book’s (the restaurant’s street address and telephone number are left out; 4호선 and 2호선 are spelled out). The answer (mine): Myeongdong-ipgu Station (Line 4) or Euljiro-ipgu Station (Line 2).

examples.translation: myeonghwadang chaja osineun gil — How to get to Myeonghwadang

examples.text: 지하철 이용시: 사 호선 명동입구역이나 이 호선 을지로입구역에서 내리시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: jihacheol iyongsi: sa hoseon myeongdongipguyeogina i hoseon euljiroipguyeogeseo naerisimyeon doemnida. — By subway: you can get off at Myeongdong-ipgu Station on Line 4 or Euljiro-ipgu Station on Line 2.

examples.text: 버스 이용시: 명동이나 외환은행 정거장에서 내리시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: beoseu iyongsi: myeongdongina oehwaneunhaeng jeonggeojangeseo naerisimyeon doemnida. — By bus: you can get off at the Myeongdong or Foreign Exchange Bank stop.

explanations.title: Giving directions to a friend (Activity 3c)
explanations.body: You want to recommend the restaurant to your friend 진수, and write the subway route he must take, using the subway map of the SMART Board activity. The book’s model begins as follows (the rest depends on the map, which is a picture; the English is mine):

examples.text: 진수야, 그 식당에 가려면, 논현역에서 먼저 칠 호선을 타고 건대입구 방면으로 가.
examples.translation: jinsuya, geu sikdange garyeomyeon, nonhyeonyeogeseo meonjeo chil hoseoneul tago geondaeipgu bangmyeoneuro ga. — Jinsu, to get to that restaurant, first take Line 7 at Nonhyeon Station and go toward Konkuk University Station.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 2 (listening to four subway announcements to say whether they are at a platform or in a train), Activity 3b (a SMART Board activity), Activity 4 (listening to subway directions from Apgujeong Station on Line 3 to Seoul Arts Center, Millennium Shopping Center, Gyeongbokgung and Lotte Department Store, and giving directions to Seoul Station, Hongik University Station, Korea University and Yongsan; the subway map is a picture) are audio, map, game or partner activities.

explanations.title: Topic C: Traffic is congested because of an accident
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is talking with a taxi driver on the way to COEX (Convention and Exhibition center) in Seoul. (The English is mine; the book writes 코엑스(COEX) and 15분, here 코엑스 and 십오 분.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 도로에 차가 왜 이렇게 많아요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: doroe chaga wae ireoke manayo? — Why are there so many cars on the road?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 지금 출근 시간이어서 교통이 아주 복잡해요. 그리고 사고가 나서 더 막혀요.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: jigeum chulgeun siganieoseo gyotongi aju bokjapaeyo. geurigo sagoga naseo deo makyeoyo. — It is rush hour now, so the traffic is very congested. And because of an accident it is even more jammed.
aendeoseun sangbyeong: yeogiseo koekseukkaji meoreoyo? — Is it far from here to COEX?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 아니요. 별로 안 멀어요. 걸어서 한 십오 분쯤 가면 돼요.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: aniyo. byeollo an meoreoyo. georeoseo han sibo bunjjeum gamyeon dwaeyo. — No. It is not very far. It takes about fifteen minutes on foot.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 여기에서 내리겠습니다. 코엑스 가는 길 좀 가르쳐 주시겠어요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureom, yeogieseo naerigetseumnida. koekseu ganeun gil jom gareucheo jusigesseoyo? — Then I will get off here. Could you tell me the way to COEX?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 여기 횡단보도를 건너서 곧장 가세요. 그리고 지하도로 내려가시면 코엑스 입구가 나옵니다.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: yeogi hoengdanbodoreul geonneoseo gotjang gaseyo. geurigo jihadoro naeryeogasimyeon koekseu ipguga naomnida. — Cross this crosswalk and go straight. And if you go down into the underpass, you will come to the COEX entrance.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 네, 감사합니다. 그런데, 오후에 제가 이태원에 가려고 하는데 코엑스에서 어떻게 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ne, gamsahamnida. geureonde, ohue jega itaewone garyeogo haneunde koekseueseo eotteoke gayo? — Yes, thank you. By the way, I am going to go to Itaewon in the afternoon; how do I get there from COEX?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 코엑스 앞에서 버스를 타세요. 지하철은 두 번 갈아타니까 버스가 더 편해요.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: koekseu apeseo beoseureul taseyo. jihacheoreun du beon garatanikka beoseuga deo pyeonhaeyo. — Take a bus in front of COEX. You have to transfer twice on the subway, so the bus is more convenient.

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic C
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter). The book lists 금지(하다 / 되다), 사고(나다) and 차도 / 차로 with the optional parts in parentheses; they are kept in the meanings here.

rows: (禁止) prohibition (~하다/되다: to forbid/to be forbidden)

(地下道) an underground passage; an underpass
(出勤) going to work (~하다: to go to work)

explanations.title: Traffic safety signs (교통 안전 표지)
explanations.body: The book shows these signs as pictures and asks you to write the English term under each sign (Presentation Activity c). The Korean names of the signs are the book’s; the English meanings are mine, except 일방통행, 횡단보도, 양보 and 터널, which are in the Core Vocabulary.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: 교통카드
explanations.body: 교통카드 is a pre-paid card for the public transportation system in Korea. You can purchase and recharge various types of 교통카드 at many kiosks, nearly all convenience stores, and subway ticket booths.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 금 (禁)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means forbid or ban, as in 금연 (no smoking; “forbidding smoke”), 금주 (no drinking; “forbidding liquor”), 출입 금지 (Do not enter), 주차 금지 (No parking), etc. The book asks: can you explain why 여학생 기숙사 (a dorm for female students) is often referred to as 금남의 집? My answer: 금남 means “forbidding men” (남 = male), so a 금남의 집 is a house where men are not allowed.

rows: a house where men are forbidden (mine); a women’s dormitory

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 도 (道)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a road or way, as in 도로 (a street; “road way”), 차도 (a road; “a road for cars”), 인도 (a walkway; “a road for people”), 하수도 (sewer; “under water way”), 상수도 (water supply; “above water way”), 태권도 (tae kwon do; “way of stepping and punching”), 유도 (judo; “way of flow”), etc. The same syllable is also used for the proper names of Korean provinces, as in 경기도 and 제주도.

rows: tae kwon do; “way of stepping and punching”

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Reading): SPC Tanner’s journal
explanations.body: The book asks you to read SPC Tanner’s journal and fill in a table in English (the positive and negative aspects of the taxi, the bus and the subway). The text is the book’s; the English is mine.

examples.text: 저는 오늘 친구들과 함께 롯데월드에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun oneul chingudeulgwa hamkke rotdewoldeue gatseumnida. — Today I went to Lotte World with my friends.

examples.text: 우리는 길을 잘 몰라서 택시를 탔습니다.
examples.translation: urineun gireul jal mollaseo taeksireul tatseumnida. — We did not know the way well, so we took a taxi.
taeksineun pyeonhaetseumnida. — The taxi was comfortable.

examples.text: 그런데 가는 길에 앞 차가 교통사고가 났습니다.
examples.translation: geureonde ganeun gire ap chaga gyotongsagoga natseumnida. — But on the way, the car ahead had a traffic accident.
chaga mani makigo bokjapaetseumnida. — The traffic was very jammed and congested.

examples.text: 택시 요금이 너무 비싸서 우리는 택시에서 내렸습니다.
examples.translation: taeksi yogeumi neomu bissaseo urineun taeksieseo naeryeotseumnida. — The taxi fare was too expensive, so we got out of the taxi.
geurigo beoseureul tatseumnida. — And we took a bus.

examples.text: 버스는 버스 전용차로로 가니까 막히지 않았습니다.
examples.translation: beoseuneun beoseu jeonyongcharoro ganikka makiji anatseumnida. — The bus went in the bus-only lane, so it was not stuck.

examples.text: 하지만 사람이 많아서 앉을 자리가 없었습니다.
examples.translation: hajiman sarami manaseo anjeul jariga eopseotseumnida. — But there were many people, so there was no seat to sit in.

examples.text: 그래서 호텔로 돌아오는 길에는 지하철을 탔습니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo hotello doraoneun gireneun jihacheoreul tatseumnida. — So on the way back to the hotel we took the subway.
jihacheoreneun sarami manko jogeum bokjapaetseumnida. — There were many people on the subway and it was a little crowded.
geureochiman kkaekkeutago ppallatseumnida. — But it was clean and fast.

examples.text: 버스와 지하철 모두 교통카드를 사용할 수 있어서 편리했습니다.
examples.translation: beoseuwa jihacheol modu gyotongkadeureul sayonghal su isseoseo pyeollihaetseumnida. — Both the bus and the subway accept the transportation card, so it was convenient.

lessons.title: 199. Ch 14 · Grammar C: ㄷ irregular verbs
lessons.subtitle: 걷다 → 걸어요 · 묻다 → 물어요 · 듣다 → 들어요 · 싣다 → 실어요 · 받다 → 받아요

explanations.title: ㄷ irregular verbs
explanations.body: There are quite a few action verbs whose stem ends in ㄷ, such as 걷다 (to walk), 싣다 (to load), and 받다 (to receive). Among these action verbs, there are a few, namely 걷다 (to walk), 묻다 (to ask), 듣다 (to hear/to listen), and 싣다 (to load), that do not follow the regular conjugation rule. When these verbs are followed by a vowel such as 아 / 어, ㄷ changes to ㄹ. They are commonly known as ㄷ irregular verbs. (The regular ㄷ verbs, such as 받다 and 믿다, keep their ㄷ.)

The answers are mine (I added the past tense and two regular ㄷ verbs, 닫다 and 얻다). Note that 믿다 and 받다 are regular.

lessons.title: 200. Ch 14 · Grammar D: a reason with -(으)니까
lessons.subtitle: 비가 오니까 · 날씨가 좋으니까 · 추우니까 · 늦었으니까 · 길이 막히니까

explanations.title: Expressing a reason using -(으)니까
explanations.body:
Like the two conjunctive endings -아서/어서 and -기 때문에, which you learned in earlier chapters, the conjunctive ending -(으)니까 is used to express a reason, and can be translated as “because” or “since”. However, -(으)니까 is normally used to express a logical reason. In 날씨가 좋으니까 산책했어요 (I took a walk because the weather was nice), 날씨가 좋으니까 is a logical reason for taking a walk; in 피곤하니까 일찍 잤어요 (I went to bed early because I was tired), 피곤하니까 is a logical reason for going to bed early.

Therefore -(으)니까 is readily followed by a request, advice, command, or suggestion that is based on a logical reason, whereas the other two conjunctive endings are not.

rows: After a verb stem ending with a vowel
After a verb stem ending with a consonant

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (1000원 → 천 원, 5번 출구 → 오 번 출구, 5명 → 다섯 명, 5분마다 → 오 분마다, 6시 → 여섯 시, 130,000원 → 십삼만 원); 몬트레이에서 PG로 → 몬트레이에서 피지로. explanations.title: What Chapter 15 teaches (한반도와 한국전쟁)
explanations.body:
Chapter 15, “The Korean Peninsula and the Korean War”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and locate provinces, major cities, and well-known tourist attractions in Korea; talk about weather; comprehend basic information about the Korean War; comprehend basic information about the Joint Security Area and its facilities in Korea; and describe a building in a simple paragraph.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -아/어지다, used to express changes of state or condition; the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데 (and; but; however); the conjunctive ending -아/어도 (even if; although); the formal blunt speech style verb ending; and the Sino-Korean syllables 해 (海) and 부 (部).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 해 (海)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means sea, as in 해군 (navy; “sea soldier”), 동해 (East Sea), 해저 (sea bottom; seabed; “sea low”), etc. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 해수, 서해, 남해 and 해병대; the answers (and the English of 해수 and 해병대) are mine.

rows: the sea bottom; the seabed; “sea low”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 부 (部)
explanations.body: The underlying meaning of this Sino-Korean syllable is a part, and it refers to one of several or many equal units which something is composed of or is divisible into. Depending on the context, 부 can be translated as a part, region, area, etc. This syllable is also used to refer to a part of an organization (company, government, school, etc.). When it is applied to an organization, it can be translated in various contexts as a department, ministry, or (school) club, as in 국방부, 환경부, 부장 and 유도부.

explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter). The book lists 남한/대한민국 and 북한/조선 민주주의 인민공화국 together; 한반도 (the Korean Peninsula) is in the book’s list of Topic A without a gloss, so its meaning is mine.

rows: (南韓 / 大韓民國) South Korea / Republic of Korea
(都市) a city; an urban area
(西海) the West Sea; the Yellow Sea
(北韓 / 朝鮮 民主主義 人民共和國) North Korea / the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK)

explanations.title: Note: 제주도
explanations.body: Jeju is the largest island and the smallest province of South Korea, located to the south of the mainland. However, Jeju is called 제주도, whether being referred to as Jeju Island or Jeju Province. 도 in 제주도 means both an island and a province, although they are from different Chinese characters: 島 (an island) and 道 (a province). So, whenever you hear a place name that ends in 도, other than 제주도, you know it could be either an island or a province.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading): sentence clues

There are nine in each of South Korea and North Korea. It is similar to a state in the United States.
이곳은 크고 사람들이 많이 산다. 뉴욕, 시카고, 엘에이 등이 이것이다.

lessons.subtitle: 전쟁기념관에 갔어요 · 따뜻해졌어요 · 영하 · 영상 · 육이오 · 휴전 · 분단 · 통일

explanations.title: Topic B: I went to the War Memorial of Korea (전쟁기념관에 갔어요)
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is talking to Jiyoung, his Korean friend, about the weather. They are on their way to the War Memorial of Korea in Yongsan, Seoul. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes −1도, 5도, 1950년 6월 25일 and 1953년; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 오늘 날씨가 많이 따뜻해졌어요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: oneul nalssiga mani ttatteutaejeosseoyo. — The weather has gotten much warmer today.

examples.text: 지영: 그래요. 어제는 최고 기온이 영하 일 도였는데 오늘은 영상 오 도예요.
examples.translation: jiyeong: geuraeyo. eojeneun choego gioni yeongha il doyeonneunde oneureun yeongsang o doyeyo. — Yes. Yesterday the highest temperature was 1 degree below zero, but today it is 5 degrees above zero.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그런데, 우리 지금 어디 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureonde, uri jigeum eodi gayo? — By the way, where are we going now?

examples.text: 지영: 용산에 있는 전쟁 기념관에 가요.
examples.translation: jiyeong: yongsane inneun jeonjaeng ginyeomgwane gayo. — We are going to the War Memorial in Yongsan.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그래요? 기념관에서 무엇을 볼 수 있어요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geuraeyo? ginyeomgwaneseo mueoseul bol su isseoyo? — Is that so? What can we see at the memorial?

examples.text: 지영: 탱크나 미사일을 구경할 수 있어요. 그리고 한국전쟁에 대해서 알 수 있어요.
examples.translation: jiyeong: taengkeuna misaireul gugyeonghal su isseoyo. geurigo hangukjeonjaenge daehaeseo al su isseoyo. — You can see tanks and missiles. And you can learn about the Korean War.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그래요? 한국전쟁은 언제 일어났어요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geuraeyo? hangukjeonjaengeun eonje ireonasseoyo? — Is that so? When did the Korean War break out?

examples.text: 지영: 천구백오십년 유월 이십오일에 일어났어요. 그래서 육이오라고 해요.
examples.translation: jiyeong: cheongubaegosimnyeon yuwol isiboire ireonasseoyo. geuraeseo yugiorago haeyo. — It broke out on June 25, 1950. That is why it is called 육이오 (“June 25”).
aendeoseun sangbyeong: hangukjeonjaenge migukdo chamjeonhaesseoyo? — Did the United States also take part in the Korean War?
jiyeong: geureomyo. migundo yuenguneuro ssawosseoyo. — Of course. The American forces also fought as United Nations forces.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 전쟁은 언제 끝났어요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureom, jeonjaengeun eonje kkeunnasseoyo? — Then, when did the war end?

examples.text: 지영: 천구백오십삼년에 휴전이 되었어요. 그리고 전쟁 후에 남한과 북한으로 분단되었어요.
examples.translation: jiyeong: cheongubaegosipsamnyeone hyujeoni doeeosseoyo. geurigo jeonjaeng hue namhangwa bukaneuro bundandoeeosseoyo. — An armistice was reached in 1953. And after the war the country was divided into South Korea and North Korea.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 한국이 빨리 통일이 되면 좋겠어요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: hangugi ppalli tongiri doemyeon jokesseoyo. — I hope Korea will be unified soon.

explanations.title: Note: 안개가 끼었습니다
explanations.body: You will hear native speakers say 오늘은 안개가 끼었습니다, meaning it is foggy today, or 오늘은 구름이 끼었습니다, meaning it is cloudy today. Because 끼었습니다 is in the past tense, you may wonder why a Korean speaker would use the past tense to describe a present weather condition when using the verb 끼다. 끼다 literally means to form. So, when you say 구름이 낍니다, using the present tense, you are saying clouds are forming now. However, when you say 구름이 끼었습니다, the sentence implies that clouds have formed in the past and, as a result, it is cloudy.

gureumi kkieotseumnida. — Clouds have formed (and, as a result, it is cloudy).

explanations.title: Expressing a change of state or condition
explanations.body: In English, when expressing a change of state or condition, we often use the verb become or get, followed by an adjective, as in “The weather got warm” or “He became happy.” In Korean, we use -아/어지다, which is attached to the stem of a stative verb. For example: 날씨가 따뜻해졌습니다 (The weather got warm).

lessons.title: 209. Ch 15 · Grammar B: background with -(으)ㄴ데/는데
lessons.subtitle: 날씨가 좋은데 · 백화점에 가는데 · 이 옷이 큰데 · 겨울인데 · 갔는데

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데
explanations.body:
The conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데 is unique in its usage. This conjunctive ending signals that the first clause is background information for (or the situation or circumstance leading to) the second clause. Therefore, we can only interpret the meaning of this conjunctive ending according to the content of the second clause. For example: 날씨가 좋은데 산책합시다 (The weather is good, so let’s take a walk); 날씨가 좋은데 집에 있을 거예요? (The weather is good, but are you going to stay home?).

Note that the same conjunctive ending is interpreted differently according to how it relates to the content of the following clause. It is interpreted as so in the first sentence and as but in the second sentence. -(으)ㄴ데/는데 can also be interpreted to mean and, and thus, and then, however, or nevertheless in other contexts. Thus, from the listener’s perspective, the exact meaning of the first clause cannot be determined until the second clause is heard. For this reason, the conjunctive ending is often used as (1) an attention getter and as (2) a stage setter for the main idea the speaker is about to deliver. As a result, this conjunctive ending is used almost exclusively in speaking.

explanations.body: The book shows a diagram of the Panmunjom Joint Security Area with these labels (the English is the book’s).

explanations.title: Cultural notes
explanations.body: Panmunjom is a portion of the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), and includes an 800-square-meter area designated as a Joint Security Area (JSA) by the UN and North Korea. Panmunjom is also called the “Truce Village” by the media. This area is outside administrative control of both South and North Korea, but is often used for diplomatic engagements between the two countries. Currently the UN and North Korea each operate six guard posts in the JSA and 35 security guards reside there. South and North Korean forces stand face-to-face in this area but cannot enter each other’s territory.

lessons.title: 211. Ch 15 · Grammar C: although and even if with -아/어도
lessons.subtitle: 어려워도 · 좋아도 · 매워도 · 멀어도 · 비가 와도 · 가도 돼요?

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -아/어도
explanations.body:
Consider the English sentences “I will learn Korean (even) though it is difficult” and “I will learn Korean even if it is difficult.” In the first sentence, the speaker knows that Korean is difficult but will learn it despite its being difficult. In the second sentence, however, the speaker does not know definitely whether or not Korean is difficult but will learn it in any event. Thus, (even) though expresses a concession and even if is a conditional.

The conjunctive ending -아/어도 is used to express both (even) though and even if. Therefore, we can express the two English sentences by using the same Korean sentence: 한국말이 어려워도 배우겠습니다. If we hear this sentence out of context, we can interpret the sentence in both ways. When a context is given, however, the meaning of the conjunctive ending is either (even) though or even if, but not both. For example:

examples.translation: oneul nalssiga joado jibe itseumnida. — Though the weather is good today, I am staying home.
naeil nalssiga joado jibe itgetseumnida. — Even if the weather is good tomorrow, I will stay home.

explanations.title: Time words show which meaning
explanations.body: Note that both sentences have a time reference (오늘 or 내일). Thus, we know that the conjunctive ending in the first sentence is understood as a concession (though or although), whereas the same conjunctive ending in the second sentence is understood as a conditional (even if).

rows: When the last syllable of a verb stem contains the vowels ㅏ or ㅗ
좋다 → 좋아도; 오다 → 오 + 아도 → 와도
When the last syllable of a verb stem contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
멀다 → 멀어도; 맵다 → 매우 + 어도 → 매워도

lessons.title: 212. Ch 15 · Grammar D: the formal blunt speech style -ㄴ다/는다/다
lessons.subtitle: 먹는다 · 간다 · 춥다 · 먹었다 · 대학생이다 · 산이 있다 · 일기 (journals)

explanations.title: The fourth speech style: formal blunt
explanations.body:
So far, you have learned about three different speech styles and their verb endings: 1. -ㅂ니다/습니다 (Formal Speech Style); 2. -아요/어요 (Informal Speech Style); 3. -아/어 (Informal Blunt Speech Style). Now you will learn a fourth: the Formal Blunt Speech Style,¹ which is indicated by the verb ending -ㄴ다/는다/다. As its name suggests, this style is used in formal and “blunt” settings. In written language, this speech style is typically employed in newspapers, journals, and books. In spoken language, this speech style is used among friends or by those of a higher status in age or rank.

¹ This style is also known as Formal Intimate, Formal Non-polite, or Formal Plain Speech Style.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: Action verbs take -ㄴ다/는다 and stative verbs take -다. The verbs 있다, 없다, 이다 and 아니다 act like stative verbs when they are conjugated into the formal blunt speech style (준호는 이제 대학생이다; 우리 고향에는 산이 있다).

explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Optional parts, such as (~하다/되다), are kept in the meanings.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (9개 → 아홉 개, 90도 → 구십 도, 15° C and 86° F → 십오 도 씨 and 화씨 팔십육 도, 1950년 6월 25일 → 천구백오십년 유월 이십오일, 1964년 → 천구백육십사년, 155마일 → 백오십오 마일, 1층 → 일 층, L.A. → 엘에이, 워싱턴 D.C. → 워싱턴 디씨); the parentheses of the book’s 86° F and 30° C are left out. explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and locate provinces, major cities, well-known tourist attractions in Korea; talk about weather; comprehend basic information about the Korean War; comprehend basic information about the Joint Security Area and its facilities in Korea; describe a building in a simple paragraph.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -아/어지다, used to express changes of state or condition; the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데 (and; but; however); the conjunctive ending -아/어도 (even if; although); the formal blunt speech style verb ending; the Sino-Korean syllables 해 (海) and 부 (部).

lessons.title: 214. Ch 16 · What the chapter teaches and the Sino-Korean syllables 불/부, 형 and 적
lessons.subtitle: 한국에서 여행하기 · 불/부 (不) · 형 (型) · 적 (的) · 불법 · 소형 · 역사적

explanations.title: What Chapter 16 teaches (한국에서 여행하기)
explanations.body:
Chapter 16, “Touring in Korea”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: make a domestic flight reservation; ask for and give information about a travel package; ask for and give information about renting a car; report simple car problems; identify simple automotive parts; and talk about well-known tourist attractions in Korea.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; 아무나 or 아무 ~(이)나 in the affirmative (any ~) and in the negative (not just any ~); -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 (know how to) and -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 (not know how to); the exclamatory verb endings -군요 and -네요; the conjunctive ending -(으)면서, used to express simultaneous actions or conditions; and the Sino-Korean syllables 불/부 (不), 적 (的), and 형 (型).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 불/부 (不)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means not or no and functions like the English prefixes in-, im-, il-, and ir-, as in inability, impossible, illegal, and irregular; for example, 불법 (illegal; “not law”), 불친절 (unkindness; “not kind”), 불합격 (failure in entrance exam; “not passing”), and 불면증 (insomnia; “no sleeping symptom”). 불 changes into 부 when the syllable comes before the consonant ㄷ or ㅈ, as in 부동산 (immovable property), 부주의 (carelessness; “no attention”), and 부족하다 (to be insufficient).

rows: failure in an entrance exam; “not passing”
inconvenience; discomfort (the book’s example in the Core Vocabulary)
impossibility (the book’s example in the Core Vocabulary)

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 형 (型)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means type or model, as in 소형 (small-size; “small type”), 구형 (old type), and 원형 (prototype; “original type”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 대형, 중형 and 신형; the answers are the book’s own meanings of the Core Vocabulary (대형, 중형) and mine (신형).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 적 (的)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable normally means a target, as in 목적 (goal; “eye target”) and 적중 (hitting the bull’s eye; “middle of target”). However, when 적 (的) is attached to a Sino-Korean noun, it functions as an “adjective maker,” just like the English suffixes -ic or -ive, as in realistic, historic, creative, active, etc. When used this way, 적 can be translated as “of (the noun)”; for example, 역사적 (historic; historical), 인상적 (impressive), 한국적 (unique to Korea), 일시적 (temporary; “of one time”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 세계적, 미국적 and 부분적; the answer for 세계적 is the book’s (world-renowned; worldwide), the others are mine.

explanations.title: Topic A: At a travel agency (여행사에서)
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is making a reservation at a travel agency for his trip to Gyeongju. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 2박 3일, 1인당 20만 원, 15만 원 and 48시간; they are spelled out here.)

The Korean words and the English glosses are the book’s; the book’s footnote says that 펑크나다/빵꾸나다 (flat tire): “This word is not standard Korean (nor is it found in a dictionary), yet it is commonly used to describe a flat tire.” (The footnote belongs to 빵꾸나다.)

explanations.title: Cultural notes: 휴게소 (highway rest stops)
explanations.body: All highways in Korea charge a toll, and drivers who leave the highway are charged again to re-enter. Thus, the Korea Expressway Corporation provides rest stops on the highways for the convenience of drivers so they don’t have to exit the highway for basic services. Therefore, if you are on a highway in Korea, you will see many 휴게소 signs. The literal translation of 휴게소 is a rest place. It is a public rest area or service area where drivers and passengers can rest, eat, refuel, and shop. Most of these rest areas have good food courts, coffee shops, convenience stores, and even auto repair shops. These days, many rest areas offer additional services such as batting cages, spas, lodging, and other amenities.

lessons.title: 219. Ch 16 · Grammar A: “any” and “not just any” with 아무나 and 아무 ~(이)나
lessons.subtitle: 아무 차나 · 아무 식당이나 · 아무나 · 아무 데나 · 아무 때나 · 아무 거나 · 아무 것도

explanations.title: Expressing “any” and “not just any”
explanations.body:
In Chapter 13, you learned about the grammar feature 아무 + (noun) + 도 followed by a negative verb, which is used to express total negation. For example: 저는 아무 문제도 없어요 (I do not have any problems); 저는 방학 때 아무 데도 안 갔어요 (I did not go anywhere during the school break).

Keep in mind that 아무 ~ 도 can work only in a negative sentence (or a sentence with a negative verb). However, when 아무 ~ takes the marker (이)나, it can work with affirmative and negative sentences, though their meanings are quite different.

examples.translation: jeoneun amu eumsigina jal meogeoyo. — I (can) eat any food.
jeoneun amu eumsigina an meogeoyo. — I do not eat just any food.
jeoneun amu keopina masyeoyo. — I drink any coffee.
jeoneun amu keopina an masyeoyo. — I do not drink just any coffee.

explanations.title: The two meanings
explanations.body: Note that 아무 ~(이)나 in an affirmative sentence (or a sentence that does not have a negative verb) translates to any ~, as in anyone, anything, any kimchi, any coffee, anywhere, etc. On the other hand, 아무 ~(이)나 in a negative sentence translates to not just any ~, as in not just anyone, not just anything, not just any kimchi, not just any coffee, not just any place, etc.

rows: 아무나 or 아무 ~(이)나 in the affirmative
아무나 or 아무 ~(이)나 in the negative
When a noun ends in a consonant
When a noun ends in a vowel

lessons.title: 220. Ch 16 · Grammar B: “know how to” and “not know how to” with -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다
lessons.subtitle: 수영할 줄 알아요 · 수영할 줄 몰라요 · 읽을 줄 알아요 · 고칠 줄 알아요 · 운전할 줄 알아요

explanations.title: Expressing “know how to” and “not know how to”
explanations.body: In English, we often use “know how to …” or “not know how to …” to express ability or inability to do something. Likewise, Koreans use the expressions -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 (know how to) and -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 (not know how to).

rows: When a verb stem ends in a vowel
수영하다 → 수영할 줄 알다 / 수영할 줄 모르다; 차를 고치다 → 고칠 줄 알다 / 고칠 줄 모르다
When a verb stem ends in a consonant
책을 읽다 → 읽을 줄 알다 / 읽을 줄 모르다; 사전을 찾다 → 찾을 줄 알다 / 찾을 줄 모르다
tables.title: verb stem + (으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다

examples.translation: suyeonghal jul arayo? — Do you know how to swim?
aniyo, jeoneun suyeonghal jul mollayo. — No, I don’t (know how to swim).
bureo ilgeul jul arayo? — Do you know how to read French?
ne, ilgeul jul arayo. — Yes, I know (how to read it).

explanations.title: Cultural notes: Buddhism and temples
explanations.body: Buddhism was introduced to the Korean Peninsula via China in 372 c.e. 절 is the native Korean term for a Buddhist temple. Each temple has its own name, which invariably ends with 사 (a temple), as in 불국사, 해인사, 법주사, etc. There are several hundred temples scattered throughout Korea, some more than 1,500 years old. (The book also shows a map titled “The Three Kingdoms of Korea”, which is left out.)
